t: peter rechem. The opening of the womb; the firstborn offspring that came out first is the peter rechem of its mother.
the firstborn of a person and the firstborn of a donkey are redeemed, and their redemption goes to the priest. Their law was explained in Hilchot Bikkurim chapters 11-12.
as we explained in the laws of the sacrificial service. 9:25.
or sells it. See below, halacha 18.
from the place from which you bring the grain tithe etc.. Terumot and ma'asrot apply by Torah law only in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Terumot 1:1).

and if he brought it etc.. Ideally he should wait until a blemish arises in a firstborn outside the Land and then eat it; and even if he transgressed and brought it into the Land, he should not offer it, but should wait until a blemish arises and eat it.
in the time of the Temple. While the Temple stands.

and it does not apply to consecrated animals while they are in their sanctity etc.. The firstborn of a consecrated animal does not have the sanctity of a firstborn, whether the animal was consecrated for the altar or for the maintenance of the Temple.

before they are redeemed. And after they are redeemed, the sanctity of a firstborn does apply to them, unless it is an animal that was consecrated for the altar while unblemished (or with a passing blemish) and afterward a permanent blemish arose, in which case it is exempt from the firstborn law even after redemption (below 5:8).
he offers its blood and its fats as we explained. Above 5:2.
as we explained in the laws of priestly gifts. Hilchot Bikkurim 11:9, 12:14.
a firstborn is eaten within its year. Within a year from the time it was fit for slaughter.
from the eighth day, when it is fit for offering. Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:8.

provided that its months were completed, for it appeared fit for eating on the day of its birth etc.. It is permitted to slaughter an offspring when it is known that its mother completed her days of gestation with its birth. But when it was born before its time, or when it is not known whether its days of gestation were completed, it is permitted to slaughter it only after eight days, and until then it is forbidden lest it be a nefel (Hilchot Ma'achalot Assurot 4:4).
a blemish arose in it within its year. It was unblemished and became blemished.
he may keep it for twelve months. Until the time by which he would have had to eat it when unblemished.
a blemish arose in it after its year. That he held it back in violation, and did not offer it within its year, or in the present time, as explained shortly (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 4:2).

a firstborn in the present time is left until a blemish arises in it and it is eaten. Since it cannot be offered, it must be left until a blemish arises, even if because of that he will delay eating it beyond its year.

and until it was examined, to show it to a sage etc.. A firstborn in which a blemish arose may be slaughtered only after it has been examined by one authorized to see and permit the blemishes of firstborns (below 3:1). If a blemish arose in the firstborn and no sage was available in that place, he may wait until a sage happens to come there and permits the firstborn for him (Rikuv, Har HaMoriah).
twelve months, from day to day. From the day one begins counting until the same date arrives a year later.
and if it was a leap year, it is added to it. He may keep the firstborn with him until the end of the year according to the date on which it was born, even though twelve months have already passed.
he transgressed and delayed the firstborn beyond its year. He transgressed the command to eat the firstborn (unblemished or blemished) within its year (above 5:8).
even though he transgresses a negative commandment. Because of "do not delay" (Tosefta, Bechorot 3:5; and see Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 14:15).

for this is no greatness for the priest; rather, its owners should tend it until it grows a little. Priestly gifts are given in a manner of honor, and the priests are honored and elevated through them; therefore it is forbidden to give them something whose raising involves toil and effort, but only finished and ready things (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 4:1).

and if the priest said to him, give it to me within this period and I will tend it myself, he may not give it to him, for this is like assisting with his gifts. Since the Israelite is obligated to tend the firstborn, the priest's offer to take the firstborn within the period counts as assistance by him in the Israelite's work, the purpose of which is to give him the gift; and priests are forbidden to assist an Israelite in order to receive his gifts (Hilchot Terumot 12:18).
and we already explained in Terumot. There, halacha 20.
that priests who assist at the threshing floors. In the work of the threshing floor in order to receive the gifts of the crop.
and in the slaughterhouses. In order to receive the gifts given from slaughtering animals.
and among the shepherds. In order to receive the firstborn of the flock.
he gives it to him. For he is not giving it to him so that he will raise it for him, but because he now wants to take it and slaughter it.

and it appears to me that a firstborn may be given to any priest he wishes. Even to an am ha'aretz (Rikuv, and unlike terumah, which is not given to a priest who is an am ha'aretz; Hilchot Terumot 6:2).
a priest who ate a k'zayit of an unblemished firstborn outside Jerusalem is flogged by Torah law. See also Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 11:5.
whether before the sprinkling. In which case it is forbidden even to priests and they too are flogged for this eating (ibid., halacha 4).

a firstborn is not redeemed. Unlike other consecrated animals, where there is a commandment to redeem them once a blemish arises and only then may they be eaten (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:10), a firstborn (and a tithe animal) is not redeemed, and after a blemish arises in them they are eaten without redemption (see ibid., halacha 12).
for since it is destined for offering, the priest has no right in it to sell it. The priest receives the firstborn for offering, but it is not considered his property.

and in the present time, when there is no Temple, since it is destined for eating etc.. Since when the Temple does not stand even an unblemished firstborn is intended for eating as ordinary food and not for offering, its law becomes that of a blemished firstborn, which is the priest's property and may be sold.
the priest may. The priest is permitted.
sell it at home but not in the market. He should not sell it in the butchers' market, as ordinary meat is sold.
as we explained in the laws of Issurei Mizbe'ach. 1:12.
but the meat of an unblemished firstborn. That was slaughtered and offered.
and priests who were counted for the firstborn. They joined together to eat the meat of the unblemished firstborn (Kesef Mishneh).

may weigh portion against portion. Although it is forbidden to sell the meat of sacred offerings, priests may divide it among themselves into equal parts and weigh its meat in a pan of a scale, piece against piece (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 5:1), but it is forbidden to weigh the meat by ordinary weighing.

if he wished to make a regel. To remove all the meat through a single hole that he makes in the leg, so that the hide comes out whole and can serve as a container for water and the like (see Hilchot Yom Tov 3:6).
and likewise other disqualified consecrated animals. That were redeemed and are eaten as ordinary food.

all the permanent blemishes that disqualify consecrated animals and on account of which they are redeemed. An animal with a blemish is disqualified from being offered on the altar, and if its blemish is a permanent one, it is redeemed and eaten as ordinary food.
if one of them fell upon a firstborn, it is slaughtered on account of it anywhere. It is slaughtered and eaten as ordinary food.

and we already explained those blemishes in the laws of Issurei Mizbe'ach. The fifty blemishes that can occur in humans and animals (detailed in Hilchot Bi'at Mikdash chapter 7), and in addition twenty-three blemishes that can occur only in animals (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:1-5).

and those that can occur in a male number sixty-seven. Of the seventy-three blemishes counted there, six do not belong here: three blemishes are not clear enough (old, sick and foul), and therefore an animal in which these blemishes arose cannot be redeemed and made ordinary, nor can a firstborn be slaughtered on account of them (see ibid., halacha 6); one blemish cannot occur in a male (a defect in the genitals of a female); the tumtum and androginos (who are also counted among the disqualifying blemishes) are not males and the sanctity of a firstborn does not apply to them at all (below, halacha 5). A total of sixty-seven blemishes remain.
and all the things we counted there in which the offering is not of the choicest etc.. For example, if the horns were cut off (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:8).
and likewise if a passing blemish occurred in the firstborn. For example, blindness that is not permanent (ibid., halacha 7).
and likewise if a transgression was committed with it. That it was mated with by a person, or mated with a person.

by one witness or on the owners' word. For in all of these, if the act was done without two witnesses the animal is not subject to the death penalty but is disqualified from being offered (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 4:2).
that was set aside or worshiped. That an act was done to set it aside for idolatry, or that it itself was worshiped as an idol (see ibid., halacha 4).
it grazes until a blemish arises in it, as we explained in the laws of Issurei Mizbe'ach. For all of these are disqualified from being offered but not fit for redemption (ibid. 2:9, 3:10).
one born by cesarean. One born through the wall of the womb by cesarean section.
and the one who comes after him. The one born after him through the womb.

neither is a firstborn. They do not have the law of a firstborn, and therefore they are not given to the priest and may be eaten even without a blemish (for a similar law in redemption of a son see Hilchot Bikkurim 11:16).
even if a female came out by cesarean etc.. The one who comes after a cesarean-born is in every case not a firstborn, and not only when the first was a male.
an androginos. One who has both male and female genitals.
and one may work with it and shear it like other ordinary animals. Unlike a firstborn, which is forbidden to shear and work even after a blemish arose in it (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:9).
a tumtum. Whose genitals are covered, so that it is not apparent whether it is male or female.

a doubtful firstborn, and it is eaten by its owners when blemished. Out of doubt it may not be eaten when unblemished, and it is forbidden to shear and work, like a firstborn; but he also need not give it to the priest, for the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow, rather the owners eat it (see also below 5:3).
whether it urinated in the male place. That the opening through which it urinates is in the place from which males (whose organ is visible) urinate.
exempt from the firstborn law. Entirely, and it is eaten by the owners even without a blemish.
and if it had some of the signs of its mother. It has a little of the appearance of its mother's species, and one can tell that it belongs to that species (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 2:5).
for there is no blemish greater than a change in its form, as we explained in the laws of Issurei Mizbe'ach. 3:5.

even a cow that gave birth to something like a donkey etc.. Although the offspring resembles a donkey, which is an impure species, if it has some of the signs of its mother it must be given to the priest and has the law of a blemished firstborn.
if it gave birth to a horse or camel type... it is a doubtful firstborn. For it resembles a species that is not subject to the firstborn law.

and if a priest seized it, it is not taken from his hand. The Israelite need not give the doubtful animal to the priest, for to receive the animal the priest must bring proof that the animal truly has the law of a firstborn (by the rule that the burden of proof is on the one who seeks to take from his fellow). But when the priest seized the animal and holds it, the law reverses, and the animal cannot be taken from his hand and returned to the Israelite unless there is proof that the animal is not a firstborn, since the Israelite also has no proof that the animal lacks the law of a firstborn (see also below 5:3).
since he committed a transgression. He violated the prohibition of inflicting a blemish on consecrated animals (see Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:7).

and it is not slaughtered on account of this blemish. His forbidden act is not effective, and one does not rely on it to permit slaughtering the firstborn; rather, one waits until another blemish arises.
he accustomed the firstborn so that a blemish would arise in it. He did something that would cause it a blemish.
who put a fig cake on its ear. He stuck a fig to the firstborn's ear so that its ear would be damaged when a dog came to eat it.
who walked it. He led it.
whether iron. For example, in a place with iron fixed in it so that it would stumble on it and be wounded (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 5:3).
and glass shards. Pieces of broken glass.
any blemish that was made with his knowledge. That he intended his actions or speech to cause the blemish.
and if it was made without his knowledge, he may slaughter on account of it. As explained shortly.
he may not slaughter on account of it. Even though he claims he did not intend to inflict a blemish.
in a narrow place fenced with wood. And the animal is forced to rub against the wood in order to eat.

even if he was a haver. A trustworthy Torah scholar who did not intend to inflict a blemish on the firstborn. In this matter the Sages did not distinguish between a haver and an am ha'aretz who is suspected of this (Babylonian Talmud, Bechorot 36a).
and even if he kicked it because it had chased him earlier. After the animal stopped chasing him, he kicked it to hurt it, but did not intend to inflict a blemish and permit it.
and likewise a gentile who acted on his own. Without being instructed.
a firstborn seized by blood. It became ill from an excess of blood, and its blood must be let for healing.

he may let blood, provided he does not intend etc.. Although letting blood might cause the firstborn a blemish, since he does not intend to cause a blemish, and perhaps no blemish will be caused at all, it is permitted to let blood (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 5:2).

it is permitted to inflict a blemish on a firstborn before it comes out into the world. Although it is forbidden to inflict a blemish on consecrated animals, since a firstborn becomes sanctified only upon leaving the womb (see Hilchot Temurah 4:12-13), it is permitted to inflict a blemish on it before that.

but when the Temple stands it is forbidden. Because it is destined for offering, and therefore one may not remove its sanctity in order to benefit from it (compare what is stated there regarding consecrating a firstborn as a peace offering, and see Babylonian Talmud, Temurah 24b).
a witness who testified from the mouth of a witness... is believed. Even though in regular testimony one may not rely on such testimony (Hilchot Eidut 17:1).
even a woman is believed. Even though she is disqualified from testifying (ibid. 9:2).
all the blemishes that can come about through human hands etc.. But for congenital blemishes and the like, which certainly come from Heaven, no credibility is needed at all (Rikuv).

where the shepherd was an Israelite and the firstborn was in the priest's hand. Since the shepherd gains nothing from the firstborn remaining to be eaten with its blemish (and one does not suspect that the priest arranged with the shepherd that he would receive a little of the meat when it remains to be eaten on his word, for the shepherd would not lie for something small; Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 5:4).

and we suspect him that perhaps he inflicted a blemish on it so that it would be given to him. Since the Israelite owner must give the firstborn to a priest, the shepherd thinks the firstborn will be given to him, and therefore he is suspected of inflicting a blemish on it so that he can eat it afterward (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
a priest who testified to another priest that this blemish arose on its own is believed. For the firstborn will remain with the priest who holds it, and the witness gains nothing from this testimony.
and we do not worry that they reciprocate for each other. We do not suspect that one gives false testimony for the other so that afterward the other will testify for him.

but his fellow may testify for him, for a person does not sin for another. Although he is suspected of inflicting a blemish for himself on his own firstborn or on an Israelite's firstborn that he shepherds, he is not suspected of giving false testimony for another priest (see also Hilchot Ma'aser 12:17).
but not his wife, because she is like himself. Just as he is not believed to testify about his own firstborn, so she is not believed.

for they were not suspected of slaughtering sacred animals outside. Priests were suspected of inflicting blemishes on firstborns, and only regarding this prohibition are they not believed. Since there is testimony that the blemish arose on its own, the priest is believed when he says that the blemish was permitted to him, for if this blemish does not permit the firstborn for slaughter, its slaughter involves the prohibition of slaughtering outside (since it is forbidden to slaughter a sacred animal outside the Temple), and regarding this prohibition the priest is believed.
because it is a sin punishable by karet, as we explained. Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 18:3.
the priest is believed to say... so that we should worry that perhaps he inflicted it. The priest is believed on this, and when he says so we do not worry that he inflicted it.
for the matter is likely to be revealed etc.. Therefore there is no concern that he is lying.
only on the word of an expert. A person who was authorized to examine firstborns and determine whether they have a permanent blemish that permits them for slaughter.
the Nasi in the Land of Israel. The head of the Sanhedrin.

and said to him, permit firstborns by their blemishes. Even if he was authorized for other matters, such as judging monetary cases and ruling on what is forbidden and permitted, if he was not specifically authorized to permit firstborns, a firstborn is not permitted on his word (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 4:3).
if there is no expert there. In that town (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 5:5).
it is slaughtered on the word of three members of the synagogue. Three laymen who regularly come to the synagogue.

and likewise a firstborn that went outside the Land. Even though it was originally in the Land and fit for offering, if it went outside the Land an expert is not needed to permit it for a clear blemish. All the more so a firstborn born outside the Land, which is not fit for offering (above 1:5), does not need an expert (see Kesef Mishneh).
it is permitted on the word of three members of the synagogue. Even when an expert is there (Rikuv).

a firstborn is not shown to an Israelite unless a priest is with him. A firstborn that is in an Israelite's possession is not permitted before it is passed to the priest, unless a priest is present with him.
for although he is not suspected of eating sacred animals outside. For he came to show it to an expert so that he will permit it.

he is suspected of robbing priestly gifts. For in slaughtering sacred animals outside there is a karet penalty, and therefore one who is trusted regarding it is not necessarily trusted regarding robbery (see also above 2:18).
therefore if he was a sage and known to be strict with himself. Then he is not suspected of robbery.

since he brought it to the expert sage, he is presumed strict with himself. For he saw himself that this firstborn is blemished, and in any case brought it to the expert as he should, so there is no concern that he would rob.

even though it is a visible blemish that does not change with slaughter. In that case the firstborn was certainly slaughtered lawfully, yet it is still forbidden because he did not show it to the expert. All the more so it is forbidden when the blemish is one that might change after slaughter.
and it is buried like a firstborn that died. It is buried like other sanctified animals that died, and it is forbidden to benefit from its flesh (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:11).
that it had one testicle and two sacs. It had two scrotal sacs with only one testicle in them. One who has a single testicle is considered blemished even though he has two sacs.
and they sat him on his haragzo and pressed it. They sat him on his buttocks and pressed that spot to check whether he had another testicle stuck inside the body.
in the loins. In the inner part of the thigh.

this is permitted, since he pressed it. Since he pressed it and the testicle did not come out, this is an organ that is permanently not in its place, and he is considered blemished even though it turned out that the testicle is attached inside (Riko).
if it was not pressed, even if it was slaughtered on the word of an expert, it is buried. For there is concern that the testicle would have come out on pressing, and then it is not blemished.
and he shall pay from his own house. The person who permitted the firstborn must pay for the firstborn that was slaughtered because of him without permission.

a quarter for small livestock and a half for large livestock. A quarter of the price of the animal he ruled could be slaughtered if it is small livestock (sheep or goats), and half its price if it is large livestock (cattle).

for they fined the owner of the animal so that he not delay it. They fined the kohen in whose possession the firstborn was for having delayed it and not offering it immediately, thereby letting it become blemished; therefore he pays half for large livestock.

and one may not raise small livestock in the Land of Israel. Since it is forbidden to raise small livestock in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:2), the law was made stricter for one who delays a firstborn of small livestock and he was fined more; therefore the inspector pays only a quarter for small livestock (Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi, Bekhorot 4:30).
one who takes payment to be an inspector of firstborn animals, we do not slaughter on his word. So that he not permit or forbid firstborn animals in order to get money.
whether a blemish was found or the animal was found unblemished. That in any case he receives the same payment for the inspection.

and he may not take payment for this animal except once... so that he not come under suspicion. For if he takes payment each time he sees a blemish on it, they will suspect that he rules an unblemished animal to be blemished so that they will bring it to him again and he will receive additional payment for it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 4:5).
one suspected regarding firstborn animals to sell them as non-sacred. Suspected of selling the flesh of an unblemished firstborn that was slaughtered improperly.

even the flesh of deer, because it resembles the flesh of a calf. Not only is it forbidden to buy the meat of a pure domestic animal, due to concern that it is firstborn meat, but also deer meat, though a deer is a wild animal and the firstborn law does not apply to it, because it resembles calf meat and there is concern that he will switch them.

even of a female, lest he cut off its male organ etc. Although a whole male hide is recognizable by the skin covering the male organ, one may not buy a hide that appears to be of a female, lest it be a male hide whose male part was cut off.
washed. Washed of dirt.
dirty. Soiled, not cleaned.
spun. Wool that was made into threads.
and felts. Cloth made of compressed wool, not by weaving.
for he is afraid to keep it with him lest the judges hear of it. And therefore he does not hold them back to prepare them, but hurries to sell them before the judges find out (Lechem Mishneh).
what they ate they ate, and he must return the money to them. Since he sold a forbidden item, he was fined to return the buyer's money, even the money for what the buyer already ate.
and so too the law for one who feeds terefah. Who misled the buyer regarding terefah meat, as though it were kosher.
as will be explained in Hilchot Mekach U'Mimkar. Hilchot Mechira 16:12. And see there halacha 14, that the same applies to any sale of something forbidden by the Torah.
if it is unblemished. And it was slaughtered as an offering.

and it is found to be terefah after the skin was flayed, it is burned as we explained in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. Since the disqualification existed before the flaying, the flaying does not permit benefit from the hide, and its law is burning (Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:9).

and the flesh is buried. The commentators found it difficult why the flesh is not burned, as with other offerings found to be terefah (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 2:11), and why there is a distinction here between the hide and the flesh (see Tosafot Yom Tov, Zevachim 12:4, Mirkevet HaMishneh, and Chazon Ish).

and if it was slaughtered on account of its blemish, the flesh is buried etc. Benefit from the flesh is forbidden, since a blemished firstborn was permitted for eating only, and when it became forbidden for eating it became forbidden for any other benefit. The hide, having been flayed before it became known that the animal was terefah, is permitted (Riko).
whether unblemished. Slaughtered as an offering.
or blemished. Slaughtered on the word of an expert.
so too one may benefit from its fleece. From the wool that is attached to it.
but any wool that was sheared from it while it was alive. Which violated the prohibition of shearing.
even if it fell off after a blemish appeared on it. Even though it was permitted by slaughter, the prohibition of shearing still remains on it (Hilchot Me'ilah 1:9).
and even after its slaughter. When its flesh is permitted to eat.
and needless to say after its death. When there is no permission to eat the flesh.
and we already explained in Hilchot Me'ilah. 1:10.

for they decreed this decree only on the firstborn and the tithe alone. But for a sin-offering or guilt-offering, which come for atonement and where there is no concern that he will delay them, even wool that fell from them while they were unblemished is permitted after their slaughter.
and we already explained that it is a mitzvah to eat it in its year. Above 1:8.
tangled wool. Loose hair that remains tangled in the attached wool.
that which looks like part of the fleece. That seems to be part of the attached wool.
this is the wool whose root is turned toward its head. The tips of the hair are turned toward the body and the roots of the hair are visible outside.
for this is like that which fell off while alive. It is evident that it is detached and is not part of the attached wool.
the fleece of a firstborn. That was sheared while alive and is forbidden for benefit.

it is an important item and renders sanctified in any amount. Generally a forbidden substance mixed with permitted is nullified in a majority. However, a forbidden item that is important is not nullified even by a large majority (Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 16:1; this refers to the fleece of a whole animal, or to the entire amount sheared at one time, which is important - Riko; and see Arukh HaShulchan, Yoreh De'ah 308:10, who distinguishes differently).

a full sit. The width of two fingers, half a tefach (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Orlah 3:2 and Rabbi Yosef Qafih's note there, and Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 13:4 with Rabbi Y. Shilat's notes there; this measure differs from the 'width of the sit', which is about two tefachim - see Hilchot Shabbat 9:7). But in less than this amount the forbidden wool in a garment is nullified (for a similar law regarding a nazirite's hair and a donkey firstborn's hair, see Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 19:12).

of the wool of sanctified animals, renders sanctified in any amount. The whole garment becomes sacred and is forbidden even with less than a full sit, until he redeems the mixed-in sacred wool (Commentary on the Mishnah, Orlah 3:3).
for if he was a partner in the cow or in the fetus. At the time of birth, the moment the firstborn becomes sanctified (for a similar law regarding a donkey firstborn see Hilchot Bikkurim 12:15).

even if the gentile had one-thousandth of the mother or the offspring. Although his share is very small, since he has a share in the whole animal (and not only in a particular organ, as later in the halacha), he is considered a partner in the entire animal, and this exempts it (Kesef Mishneh).
and if it is possible to cut off the gentile's limb without disqualifying it. Such as the horns, the hooves, or extra flesh (Riko).
one who buys the fetus of a gentile's cow. Buys the fetus before its birth.

or one who sells the fetus of his cow to a gentile, even though he is not permitted. For by selling it to a gentile he removes the firstborn sanctity it could have had (see Bavli Bekhorot 2a and Tosafot there).
and we do not fine him for this. We do not require him to buy the fetus back from the gentile and give it to the kohen.
a gentile who received [animals] from a Jew in this way. That a gentile tends a Jew's animals and they divide the offspring between them.
one who receives sheep from a gentile for a fixed sum. That the price of the animals was set at the time of receipt.

and stipulated with him that the profit be split between them, and if they decreased in value, the loss is the Jew's. The Jew must return the price of the animals as set at the time of receipt, and if there is a loss he makes it up from his own money, and if there is profit the gentile and the Jew divide it equally.
for they are in the Jew's possession and are as his acquisition. For he received them at a fixed price and took responsibility for them.

since if the gentile finds no money with him to collect, he will collect from these animals and their offspring etc. Although the gentile has a monetary claim against the Jew (the price of the flock he gave and his share of the profit) and does not own the animals, if the Jew does not pay him he would prefer to collect from the animals themselves and from their offspring, which were originally his (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 2:4). Therefore the flock and the offspring are considered animals in which the gentile has a partnership, and those born to them are exempt from the firstborn law.

but the offspring of the offspring are obligated, for they belong to the Jew and the gentile has no claim to them. Those born to the offspring are considered, from the gentile's standpoint, like the rest of the Jew's property, and he would not specifically collect from them. Therefore they are considered a Jew's animals, whose offspring are subject to the firstborn law.

and he acquired for himself an animal from a gentile by their laws... and likewise if the gentile bought from a Jew by their laws. According to the laws of acquisition from a gentile and sale to a gentile (Bavli Bekhorot 13a), which is done by payment even without meshicha (pulling) (Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 1:14).

and it is not known whether it had given birth or not. It is not known whether it already gave birth in the gentile's possession, or whether the offspring it now bears in the Jew's possession is the firstborn.

it is a doubtful firstborn and is eaten with its blemish by the owners and does not go to the kohen. Since it may be a firstborn, it may not be eaten unblemished, and it is forbidden to shear it or work with it. On the other hand, it need not be given to the kohen, and certainly may not be offered, since it is not certain that it is indeed a firstborn.

for the one who seeks to take from his fellow bears the burden of proof. One cannot extract money on the basis of doubt, without certainty ('proof') that it belongs to the claimant (see also below 5:3).

if he bought a nursing animal from a gentile, he need not worry that perhaps it is nursing another's offspring. For an animal does not nurse at all if it has not given birth (though after giving birth it may nurse even the offspring of others - Bavli Bekhorot 24a).
rather, it is presumed to have given birth. And the offspring it bears is not a firstborn.

an animal that gives milk is exempt from the firstborn law. Even if it is not known that it gave birth, since it has milk it is presumed to have given birth already, and the offspring born to it is not a firstborn.

for a Jew may not stay silent and cause him to eat sacred meat outside. For if this animal has not yet given birth and the seller does not tell the buyer that the offspring it bears will be a firstborn, the buyer will slaughter and eat the firstborn as non-sacred outside the Temple courtyard.

small livestock that miscarried a fetus whose form was not yet very distinct and was not recognizable to all etc. Even a miscarried fetus that was not fully developed exempts the offspring born after it from the firstborn law. Therefore one must ask knowledgeable shepherds whether what the animal miscarried was a fetus, and if so, the animal was exempted by it from the firstborn law.
even if it was young and gave birth with him within its year. Surely it had not given birth before.
afterbirth. The membrane in which the fetus is found.
sign of an offspring. Evidence that there was an offspring here.
and it is permitted to throw that afterbirth to the dogs. Though if we knew for certain that it was the afterbirth of a firstborn, it would have to be buried.
and we already explained that a male that has none of its mother's features is not sanctified as a firstborn. Above 2:6.
but a sanctified animal that miscarried an afterbirth, it must be buried. The afterbirth is forbidden for benefit and must be buried (see also Hilchot Temurah 4:10).
for in this case males are like females. And therefore most miscarried fetuses are sacred.
a clot of blood. A piece of blood.

for it is presumed that the offspring was in it and the blood overcame it and ruined and nullified it. Although no form of an offspring is seen in this piece, it is presumed that it had the form of an offspring, but the clot of blood spoiled it and nullified its form.
even though this clot has no sanctity. For only a minority of offspring have firstborn sanctity (as explained above, halacha 10, regarding the afterbirth).
in order to publicize that it has been exempted from the firstborn law. However, an afterbirth needs no publicity, since everyone knows there is no afterbirth without an offspring (Riko).
we already explained regarding niddah. Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:1-2.
for the fetus in a human is completed in forty days. From conception; before then it is not considered a fetus.

but regarding an animal's offspring the Sages did not determine the number of days in which it is completed. See below halacha 13 for the size that makes the fetus count as an offspring that exempts from the firstborn law.
but they said that a miscarriage is filth. If that filth was a fetus.

it does not conceive after it, nor receive another offspring, for less than thirty days. Therefore if it conceived within less than thirty days, it is a sign that the filth was not a complete fetus and does not exempt from the firstborn law.
that went out full and came back empty. Went out to pasture pregnant and returned without a fetus, and they did not see what it miscarried.
perhaps it miscarried something that does not exempt from the firstborn law. A fetus whose formation was not completed.
and miscarried animals have no exemption of the womb. A miscarried fetus is not considered a complete fetus that exempts the offspring born after it from the firstborn law.
until they round the head like the kefika of the weft. Until the roundness of their head is as large as a ball of weft threads (which are thicker than warp threads, and whose ball is larger).
a firstborn-bearing animal having difficulty giving birth. And so that it not die, the limbs of the fetus must be cut and removed from its womb.

he cuts it limb by limb and throws it to the dogs. Since he removes the limbs one by one, and not the majority of the animal together, the limbs do not become sanctified; therefore it is permitted to benefit from them and they need not be buried.

and the one that comes after it is a firstborn. Since no offspring came out of this animal at all, but only limbs, the next offspring is a firstborn. But in a case where an offspring came out through the side, or it miscarried an offspring, even filth or a clot of blood that had been an offspring - since a whole offspring came out of it, it is exempt from the firstborn law (Riko).

and if he cut off a limb and left it, and cut off a limb and left it, until he completed the majority of it. He left the limbs and did not throw them to the dogs until most of the animal's limbs were lying before him.

once its majority has come out... and it is before us, it is retroactively sanctified. Since all the limbs exist, they combine together, and so even the limbs that came out first and were not sacred now become retroactively sanctified and require burial, and the one born afterward does not become a firstborn.

if a third came out and he sold it to a gentile, and another third came out, it is retroactively sanctified. For when the majority came out it became retroactively sanctified, and it turned out that the sale is not a sale (since a sanctified firstborn is not his property), so there is no gentile partnership in this animal that would exempt it from the firstborn law.

one third came out through the side and two thirds through the womb. First he took out a third of the animal through the side of the womb (by Caesarean section), and afterward the remaining two thirds came out through the opening of the womb.

it is not sacred, for the first majority did not come out through the womb, and it is retroactively sanctified. The sanctity of the offspring depends on the first majority to emerge ('it is sanctified retroactively'), and since this majority did not emerge through the womb the offspring is not sanctified, even though in the end two thirds of the offspring came out through the womb (Rashi, Chullin 69b).

a minority of a large limb came out, and this is the majority of the fetus that came out. The majority of the animal came out through the womb, and part of this majority is a small part of a large limb whose majority is still in the mother's innards.

it is exempted from the firstborn law and what came out is buried. For the majority of the fetus came out, and we do not say that the minority of the limb that came out is drawn after its majority inside, so that it turns out that the majority did not come out.

half of the fetus came out, and it is the majority of a limb that came out. Only half of the fetus came out, and part of this half is part of a limb whose majority already came out and whose minority is still inside.

this is a doubt whether it is exempted from the firstborn law or not. It is doubtful whether the minority of the limb is drawn after its majority and is considered as though the majority of the animal had already come out (Bavli Chullin 70a).
a firstborn that he wrapped in fibers. While still in the womb he wrapped it in palm fibers tightly tangled together (siv is the covering on a palm, like a woven cloth).
its sister. A female born with it.

since it did not touch the womb at all, it is a doubtful firstborn. In all these cases the firstborn did not touch the opening of the womb when it came out, and there is doubt whether, having passed through the opening of the womb without touching it, it is considered a firstborn.
he joined two wombs. Of two animals.
and it came out of this one and entered that one. And afterward it came out through the opening of the second.
for it has opened the womb. Its womb opened and an offspring came out through it.

the walls of the womb were diminished. Reduced, so that the offspring does not touch the walls of the womb as it comes out (see Rashi, Chullin 70a, who had the reading 'were opened' and explained that the walls of the womb widened; some had this reading in the Rambam too).
the walls of the womb were uprooted at its neck. The walls of the opening of the womb were uprooted from their place and hang inside at the neck of the womb.

this is a doubt whether it sanctifies in its place or sanctifies even outside its place. It is doubtful whether the offspring is sanctified when leaving the opening of the womb only if it is in its natural place, or not.
the walls of the womb were cut around. Cut around on the inside, while the outer rim remained intact (Rabbenu Gershom, Chullin 70a, and see Rashi there).
part of them was breached and the remainder stands greater than the breach. Part of the walls of the womb was cut, and the remaining part is greater than the breached part.

the kohen takes the leaner one and the second is a doubtful firstborn. Because of the doubt both are treated under the law of a doubtful firstborn, but only one need be given to the kohen, the leaner one, which is worth less, since the one who seeks to take from his fellow bears the burden of proof.
therefore the kohen gets nothing. For if the female came out first, both are non-sacred.

two males and a female, the kohen takes the leaner one and the second is a doubtful firstborn. It is possible that both males are firstborn, and possible that only one is a firstborn and the other was born after the female or after the other male. Therefore both have the law of a doubtful firstborn, and the kohen takes the leaner one.

two females and a male, or two males and two females, were born. It is possible that the two females were born first and none is a firstborn, and possible that the two males were born first and both have firstborn status. Therefore both have the law of a doubtful firstborn, and the kohen takes none at all.
its law is that it grazes until a blemish falls on it. It may not be eaten unblemished as a firstborn.
and it is eaten by its owners. And it need not be given to the kohen, for the one who seeks to take from his fellow bears the burden of proof.
if the kohen seized it, we do not take it from his hand. Since he seized the firstborn, he became the one holding it, and to take it from him one needs proof that it is not a firstborn.
rather it is presumed that each one nurses her own offspring. And if so, the males were born to those that are not firstborn-bearers, and all are non-sacred.
and one of them died. And it is not known whose died.

the second shepherd leaves it among them and departs. This refers to a case where they were deposited with him without his knowledge. But if they were left with his knowledge, he should have known whose died, and since he was negligent and did not know whose died, he must pay them with another animal (Lechem Mishneh, based on Hilchot Sheelah U'Pikadon 5:4, end).
the one who seeks to take from his fellow bears the burden of proof. The living animal remains with the owner and is a doubtful firstborn.

Israelites are not suspected regarding firstborn animals etc. Unlike kohanim (above 2:17), Israelites are not suspected of inflicting a blemish on a firstborn, even a doubtful firstborn that they are entitled to eat. An Israelite is also trusted to say that it is a doubtful firstborn, and is not suspected of its being a definite firstborn that he must bring to the kohen (Riko, but see Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi, Bekhorot 5:47).
and they examine its blemish for him. And he need not bring proof that the blemish occurred by itself.

all sanctified animals in which a permanent blemish preceded their sanctification and were redeemed are subject to the firstborn law etc. The firstborn law does not apply to an animal of sacred offerings, and while it is sacred, before being redeemed, its offspring does not become a firstborn (above 1:6). After the animal is redeemed there is a difference between the cases: if at the time of consecration the animal had a permanent blemish, it was not sanctified with body-sanctity at all, so after redemption it becomes completely non-sacred and its offspring is a firstborn. If it had no permanent blemish at the time of consecration, it was sanctified with body-sanctity, so even after its redemption it did not fully become non-sacred, and its offspring has no firstborn status.
for they did not become non-sacred for every purpose. But only for the purpose of eating them.
as we explained in Hilchot Me'ilah. 1:9.
one who buys an animal with maaser sheni money in Jerusalem. He bought an animal for eating with maaser sheni redemption money and it gave birth; its offspring has firstborn status.
for he may not trade in shemitah produce. Hilchot Shemitah 6:1.

and if it is subject to the firstborn law, he profits through the firstborn, since it has left the status of shemitah produce. When food is bought with shemitah produce, the sanctity of shemitah attaches to it (Hilchot Shemitah 6:1). Therefore an animal bought with shemitah produce is exempt from the firstborn law: if its offspring had firstborn status, the sanctity of shemitah would not apply to it, and he would profit by not having to treat the firstborn with shemitah sanctity.
we already explained in Hilchot Issurei Ma'achalot. Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 8:16.
and so we explained in Terumot. 12:21.
and likewise it is forbidden to trade in firstborn animals. To buy in order to sell and profit.

although it is permitted to sell them in the manner we explained. It is permitted to sell when not doing so for commercial purposes (as in the examples in the next halacha), and then one must sell subject to the restrictions mentioned above 1:17-18.

we do not appraise unblemished firstborn animals for Israelites. That they raise the firstborn animals and share with the owners the increase in the meat's value at the time of slaughter. The reason is that this is considered commerce.

but we do appraise blemished firstborn animals for them. Since they are permitted to Israelites for eating, it is not considered commerce but a partnership in the firstborn for the purpose of eating it (Tokhen Peirush, Bava Metzia p. 210).

and we appraise unblemished firstborn animals for kohanim in the present day, since they are destined to be eaten with their blemish. The commentators found it difficult why in the present day we may not appraise unblemished ones for Israelites (see Rabbi Yom Tov Algazi, Bekhorot 5:37). Some explained that the reason is that this involves disrespect to sacred things (Riko).
only for cattle and flock alone. And not for pure wild animals (Arukh HaShulchan 201:7).
applies to non-sacred animals but not to sanctified ones etc. For a similar law regarding a firstborn see above 1:5-6.
it is slaughtered in the Temple courtyard. Like other lesser sacrifices, which are slaughtered anywhere in the courtyard (Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot 5:2).
and its blood is sprinkled once against the base. On one of the corners of the altar where there is a base (ibid. 5:17).
and its fats are burned and the rest of the flesh is eaten by the owners in Jerusalem. Ibid. 9:25.
like other lesser sacrifices. Which are eaten throughout Jerusalem, and their time of eating lasts until sunset on the day after the offering (ibid. 10:5-6).
if it was blemished... it is eaten anywhere. Like a firstborn (above 1:3).
even the prohibition of sale is included. Not only the prohibition of redemption.

like one who sells cherem of kohanim. When one declared his property cherem for the kohanim, it is forbidden to sell or redeem it, and it must be given to the kohanim (Hilchot Arachin VeCharamin 6:4).

and like one who sells a beautiful captive woman, as will be explained in its place. One who takes a captive woman from war may marry her, and is forbidden to sell her, and her sale is not effective (Hilchot Melachim 8:6).

one does not weigh a portion against a portion with the tithe as is done with the firstborn. Although an unblemished firstborn may not be sold, they permitted dividing its meat among the kohanim by placing a piece on one pan against a piece on the other (above 1:18). But with the tithe they did not permit even this, since such a division looks like a sale (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 5:1).
and the animal tithe of orphans that was slaughtered with its blemish. And there is no longer a Torah prohibition against selling it.
because of returning lost property to orphans, they did not decree against it. For if they do not sell the meat, it will spoil and rot.

it is permitted to sell its fat, sinews, hide and bones. For these parts are not fit for eating, and are not within the category of the tithe meat that was forbidden to sell (Rabbenu Gershom, Bekhorot 31b).

and if he absorbed the price of the flesh into the price of the hide, fat and sinews and sold everything by absorption. He sold the flesh together with the bones and did not receive separate payment for the flesh.

and if the price of the bones was high and he absorbed the price of the flesh into the price of the bones, it is permitted. But if the price of the bones is very low and their price is negligible relative to the meat, one may not absorb the sale of the meat into them.
this blemish came by itself and was not made deliberately. For if he inflicted a blemish on it deliberately, one may not slaughter on account of this blemish, as with a firstborn (above 2:6).

even those who are not trusted regarding the firstborn are trusted regarding the tithe. Regarding a firstborn, the kohanim who own the firstborn were suspected of inflicting a blemish on it in order to eat it (above 2:17), and with the tithe there is no such concern.
and a person may examine the blemishes of his own tithe and permit it. But with a firstborn even an expert may not permit his own (above 3:1).

for if he wished he could inflict a blemish on his whole flock and afterward tithe. Before he tithes his animals they are non-sacred, and there is no prohibition against inflicting a blemish on them as there is with a firstborn and sanctified animals. Therefore, since if he wanted to remove the tithe sanctity from his animals he could inflict blemishes on them before tithing them, he is trusted to say that it fell by itself, and is also trusted to permit it for himself.
until they are born in his possession. He is obligated to tithe only those born in his possession.

partners who became partners in animals, and this one brought a hundred lambs etc. Although before the partnership each of them was obligated to tithe his animals, after they became partners all the lambs are considered as if sold from one to the other, and are exempt from the tithe.
and likewise brothers who inherited lambs from their father are exempt from the tithe. For the animals were not born in their possession.

but those born to them in partnership afterward from these animals... are obligated in the tithe. Since they are in the possession of the owners at whose place they were born, they are obligated even though they are partners (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 9:3).

if brothers or partners divided after the animals were born in their possession, and then became partners again, they are exempt from the tithe. When they divided, the animals born to them before the division became exempt (since division is considered a sale - Riko, Lechem Mishneh), and when they became partners again, the animals born to each of them while they were divided also became exempt.
and even though they divided kids against kids etc. And we do not say that each received the share he already owned, but we treat such a division as a new acquisition of the animals.

if they divided the money and did not divide the animals, they are obligated in the tithe. Although they showed their intent to dissolve the partnership, since they have not yet divided the animals they are obligated in the tithe of the animals born to them after they inherited from their father or became partners.

regarding the stolen property of a convert. One who robs a convert and swears that he did not rob him, and afterward the convert dies without heirs, the robber must pay the kohanim the value of the theft plus a fifth (Hilchot Gezelah 8:5).
and we already explained that what is given as a gift is exempt from the tithe. Above halacha 10.
and all altar prohibitions. Such as an animal set aside for idolatry, an animal that copulated with a human or was copulated with, and the like.
diverse kinds (kilayim). The offspring of mating two kinds of animal.
and the terefah. A wound or defect due to which the animal is liable to die (for details of terefot see Hilchot Shechitah chapters 5-10).
and one born by the side (yotzei dofen). Born by Caesarean section.
and one lacking time. An animal during the first seven days after its birth, whose time for offering has not arrived (Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 3:8).
and likewise the orphan whose mother died or was slaughtered at its birth. For the two did not live together (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 9:4).
by oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in expounding the verses (see Commentary on the Mishnah there).
that it became fit. That it became suitable.
for one lacking time is not fit to be tithed. For it is not fit for an offering.
it is as if he bought fetuses and they were born in his possession. So he is obligated to tithe them (above halacha 12).
these are not tithe. Since the separation must be done by counting the animals.
that it pass by itself. By the sound of its mother.
with the rod. A stick.
he marks it with red dye. Colors it red.
sixteen mil. About fifteen kilometers.

nine on this side and nine on that side and one in the middle. The middle one joins with the nine on each side to form a complete flock. But if there were five on one side and five on the other and one in the middle, since the animals on each side with the middle one are not a complete flock, it does not combine them (Riko and Kesef Mishneh, based on Bavli Bekhorot 55a).

the term 'flock' means one flock, for both are called 'seh'. The word 'tzon' in the verse refers to all kinds of flock, sheep and goats, since both are also called 'seh' (see, e.g., Deuteronomy 14:4).
as it says, 'that which the field produces, year by year'. From this we learn that terumah must be separated from each year's produce separately (Hilchot Terumot 5:11).
this is tithe, because of the severity of sanctified things. Since he called it by the name 'tithe', it became sanctified.
for the Torah did not explicitly insist that animal tithe be year by year. Rather they learned this from the tithe of the land.
all those born from the first of Tishrei until the twenty-ninth of Elul combine. For the new year for animal tithe is on the first of Tishrei (Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1).
if those born gave birth within their year etc. If the females born this year gave birth before they were tithed, they must be tithed together with their offspring.
the tevel. Food from which terumah and tithes have not yet been separated.
which it is forbidden to eat until he tithes, as we explained in its place. Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 10:19.

the tithe shall be holy and shall be eaten according to its law, as we explained. Before he tithes, it is permitted to sell and slaughter, even from flocks that have become obligated in tithe; and when he tithes, the tithe becomes an offering and must be slaughtered in the courtyard and eaten in Jerusalem (above 6:4).
Atzeret. Shavuot.
the Festival. Sukkot.

each of these times is called the threshing floor of animal tithe. Threshing floor (goren) is the completion of grain processing, after which it is forbidden to eat the grain without terumot and tithes. Similarly, the time when the animals became forbidden is called a goren (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 9:5).
and on the thirty-fifth day of the counting of the Omer. Fifteen days before Shavuot, which is on the fiftieth day of the counting of the Omer.
for it is permitted to sell before he tithes, as we explained. Above halacha 7.

they would refrain from selling until they tithed and performed the mitzvah. Animal owners would not sell their animals before tithing them, so as not to lose the mitzvah, and since these times were set for tithing, everyone would tithe and sell their animals at these times.
until fewer than ten remained in the pen. After he tithed the tenths that left the pen, fewer than ten animals remained in the pen.
and all will be tithed in one threshing floor. The next time he tithes his animals this year.

even though he knows that these will remain uncounted, he must bring all into the pen and the remainder will remain. Although when he brings them into the pen he knows that after he counts and tithes all the tenths a few single animals will remain, nevertheless he must bring all his animals into the pen and may not leave some of them outside according to the number of animals that will not be tithed in any case.
and he counts as we explained. Above 7:1.
all three are sanctified. The ninth and the eleventh, since he called them 'tenth', and the tenth, although he called it 'ninth', became sanctified by itself, since it is the tenth.
the ninth is not offered but is eaten with its blemish. We wait for a blemish to fall on it and then eat it like any blemished tithe.
and the eleventh is offered as a peace offering. Since the tenth became sanctified as tithe, the eleventh does not become tithe but a peace offering.
and requires libations like a peace offering. Unlike the tithe, which does not require libations. All the procedures of its offering are done as for a peace offering.

and it does not effect temurah, because it itself is like a temurah. One who exchanges a non-sacred animal for a sacred animal (says that a non-sacred animal should become sanctified in place of a sacred animal): the sacred animal retains its sanctity, and the non-sacred animal becomes sacred through it. This law applies only to an animal that was consecrated directly; an animal that itself became sanctified through temurah cannot cause another animal to become sanctified through it (Hilchot Temurah 1:15). The eleventh animal, which became sanctified as a peace offering by being called 'tenth', is considered a temurah animal, so if one exchanges a non-sacred animal for it, it will not become sanctified.
for he did not make him an agent to err and cause loss. See Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 1:2.

when he called the tenth 'ninth'. Only when he called the actual tenth by another name can the calling of 'tenth' sanctify the eleventh; but when the actual tenth was already called by its name, calling the eleventh 'tenth' has no effect.
the ninth and tenth came out as one. And it is not known which came out first.

whether he called both 'tenth' or called both 'ninth', both are sanctified and are eaten with their blemish. When he called both 'tenth', the ninth is sanctified and its law is to be eaten with its blemish, while the tenth is tithe. But since it is not known which of them is the tenth, both are eaten with their blemish. And when he called both 'ninth', the tenth is sanctified by itself as tithe while the ninth is non-sacred, but since it is not known which of them is the tenth, out of doubt both are treated as tithe and are not offered but are eaten with their blemish (Riko).

the tenth and eleventh came out as one; if he called them 'tenth' etc. Although it was explained above (halacha 3) that after he called the tenth 'tenth' the eleventh is not sanctified, when both came out together the eleventh also becomes sanctified, and its law is that of a peace offering (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bekhorot 9:8).

they are like tithe that got mixed with peace offerings, which are eaten with their blemish. They cannot be offered, since it is not known which is the tithe and which the peace offering. Their law is that they graze until a blemish falls on them, and he redeems the peace offering (although he does not know which is the peace offering, he redeems without specifying, and the redemption takes effect on the peace offering), and eats both as blemished tithe.
as we explained in Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin. 6:14.
and if he called them 'eleventh'. The tenth became sanctified by itself, and the eleventh is non-sacred since he called it 'eleventh'.
the tenth and the non-sacred one are mixed together and are eaten with their blemish. After a blemish falls on them, he eats them as blemished tithe.
and he counted them as one. He counted them as one pair.
the ninth and the tenth are sanctified. The animals he called 'ninth' and 'tenth', which are the tenth and the eleventh that came out.

and they are eaten with their blemish. Although in a case where he erred in counting and called the tenth 'ninth' and the eleventh 'tenth', the tenth is offered as tithe and the eleventh is offered as a peace offering (above halacha 2), in this case, where he counted two of the first ones as one, there is doubt whether they are truly considered two or one, and so they are not offered at all (Riko, based on Rashi and Tosafot, Bekhorot 60a).
and one who calls the eleventh 'tenth', it is sanctified as we explained. Above halacha 2.
for the tenth is sanctified by itself. Even if it was not explicitly called 'tenth'.
the ninth is eaten with its blemish. As above, halacha 2.

and the one remaining in the pen is tithe even though it did not come out etc. The tenth is sanctified when it remains alone in the pen after nine have gone out, even before leaving the pen and without being called 'tenth'.

the ninth is eaten with its blemish, and all eight that came out and were counted are exempt etc. Although the tenth died before it came out, since at the time of counting there were ten animals, among which the tenth was fit to be sanctified, the counting exempted them from the tithe obligation (see also below halacha 10).

and all eight that came out and were counted are exempt, even though their tenth was not sanctified to be offered. Although the tenth is sanctified by itself (as explained at the beginning of the halacha), in any case it had no practical possibility of being offered since it died, and one might have thought that it does not exempt the rest (Riko).

for a count that is fit for tithing exempts. When there are enough animals to separate a tithe from them, every animal he takes out and counts is exempted at the time of counting, even if ultimately the tithe was not separated.
as we explained. Above halacha 8.

and those in the pen he leaves for another threshing floor until they combine with others. After the one died, the animals that remained in the pen are not fit for tithing, and he must tithe them together with his other animals the next time he tithes.

and four went out and he counted them at this opening, and six went out and he counted them from another opening. These counts are valid, since at the time of counting enough animals remained to complete a tithe.
if the four remaining went out of the opening through which the six went out, he takes one of them and all are exempt. For the last four too were counted in a valid count.

but these four that remained, even though they went out and were counted from the first opening, it is not a valid count etc. Since the animals that went out first cannot complete a count of ten with the four that remained, this count is not valid and does not exempt the last four.

if the six went out through one of the two openings, he takes one of them as tithe and all are exempt. When all the last six went out through the same opening, they completed ten with those going out through that opening, and one of them is tithe; and the four that went out first through the other opening are also exempt, since they were counted in a valid count.

and if the six went out through two openings, the six combine with another threshing floor.
